title: τίς and τις: interrogative and indefinite

objectives.can: Tell the interrogative τίς from the indefinite τις and parse either.

explanation.summary: Two small words with the same letters do opposite jobs. τίς asks a question ('who? which? what?'); τις points to someone or something without naming it ('someone', 'a certain'). Only the accent, and the sentence, tell them apart.

sections.heading: One set of endings, two words
body: Both words decline like third-declension nouns with the stem τιν-. The masculine and the feminine have the same form; the neuter is different. In the singular: nominative τίς (masculine, feminine) and τί (neuter), genitive τίνος, dative τίνι, accusative τίνα and τί. The indefinite has the same endings without the accent: τις, τι, τινος, τινι, τινα. Plural forms such as τίνες and τινες are less common.
Because masculine and feminine look alike, a form like τίς can be read as masculine or feminine only from the context, for example from a noun it goes with.

sections.heading: Telling them apart: the accent
body: The interrogative always has an acute accent on its first syllable: τίς, τί, τίνος, τίνα. It does not change to a grave accent when another word follows.

The indefinite is an enclitic: a short word that leans on the word before it and has no accent of its own. So it is normally written without one: τις, τι, τινος. It cannot stand first in its clause, so a τις at the start of a sentence is the interrogative. The indefinite may still show an accent when the word before it gives it one (you will see forms such as τινές and τινά in the text), and the word before it may show an extra accent for the same reason, as ἄνθρωπός does in ἄνθρωπός τις. In those cases the sense of the sentence has to settle the matter.

sections.heading: What they mean
body: Interrogative τίς: 'who?' when it stands alone as a person, 'which?' or 'what?' before a noun (τίς ὁ λόγος οὗτος, 'what is this word?'). Neuter τί: 'what?' In many questions τί is best translated 'why?': Matthew 8:26 asks τί δειλοί ἐστε; 'Why are you afraid?'. This is a use of the neuter, and the context shows when it is wanted.

Indefinite τις: 'someone', 'anyone', 'a certain', 'some'. With a noun it often marks a person or thing as one among others, without describing it: ἄνθρωπός τις is 'a certain man', which is how a story can begin. τι is 'something' or 'anything'. The Greek has no word for 'a', so τις sometimes plays the part of an indefinite article, but it is more definite than the English 'a' when it means 'a certain'.

sections.heading: Questions that expect an answer
body: In printed texts a direct question ends with the Greek question mark (;), and often contains a question word such as τίς or τί. Some questions begin with a negative that shows what the speaker expects. A question introduced by οὐ or οὐχί usually expects the answer 'yes': Luke 24:26 begins οὐχί, 'Was it not necessary…?'. A question introduced by μή or μήτι usually expects 'no', or shows doubt.

John 4:33 has both of this lesson's words in one sentence: Μή τις ἤνεγκεν αὐτῷ φαγεῖν; The disciples ask, 'Surely no one has brought him something to eat?' μή shapes the expected answer; τις is the indefinite 'anyone'. These words signal what the speaker expects. They do not prove what the answer is.

misunderstandings: Reading the accent as optional. τίς and τις are different words, and a missing or added accent changes the meaning.
Treating τις as the English article 'a'. It means 'a certain', 'some' or 'anyone', and a Greek noun can be indefinite without it.
Assuming that τί always means 'what'. Before a verb it is often 'why'. Check whether a thing or a reason is being asked for.
Thinking that a question with μή proves the answer is 'no'. It tells you what the speaker expects, and speakers are sometimes wrong.

deeper.heading: Accent in practice
body: Enclitics are complicated, and printed editions do not always agree on where to put an accent. In 2 Corinthians 11:16 the text has μή τίς με δόξῃ ('let no one think me…'). The analysed text reads this τίς as the indefinite, not as a question, because no question is asked. When the accent and the sense disagree, follow the sense of the sentence.
